name: transform-view
intent: Renders domain data into markup by transforming it element by element, so that presentation becomes an ordinary program (or stylesheet) that can be tested, reused and streamed independently of the request-handling machinery.
problem: A response must be generated from domain data, but the page is not static-with-holes: the markup structure depends on the data (nested lists and tables, conditional sections, machine-consumed XML), so marker-based templates and inline scripts cannot express the transformation cleanly, and placing it in the controller couples presentation to request handling.
context: Server-side rendering where the output is produced, not authored: data arrives as domain objects or record sets and must be serialized to HTML, XML or another text format; the team controls the transformation code and accepts that layout lives in code rather than in designer-editable templates. Also the natural fit when the same data must be emitted in several formats or channels, and when the language ships an XSLT processor or a markup tree API.
benefits: Separation of concerns: the transformation from domain data to markup is its own unit, independent of request routing, HTTP handling and the controller that invokes it.
Testability: a transformer is an ordinary function or object - feed it a domain object and assert the markup, with no container, template engine or HTTP round-trip in the test.
Full expressive power for structural markup: conditionals, iteration, recursion and helper composition are the host language's own, which matters when the markup shape follows the data shape.

Reuse across callers and formats: the same domain object can be rendered by different transformers (HTML, XML feed, plain text), and the same transformer can be invoked by different controllers or endpoints.
Streaming and bounded memory: element-by-element emission can write straight to the response or an output stream, so large pages do not need a fully materialized DOM.
When realized as XSLT, the stylesheet is a separate artifact that can be changed and redeployed without recompiling the application code.
tradeoffs: Markup construction in code is verbose and escaping is manual: every text and attribute write must be encoded consistently, or output breaks and injected user data becomes an XSS hole.
Layout lives in code: web designers cannot edit the view, and every visual change is a developer task plus a build or redeploy (XSLT softens this but adds its own tooling).

Coupling to the data shape: transformers know the domain structure (or the serialized XML shape under XSLT), so domain refactors ripple through every transformer, and the XSLT route adds a serialization layer that must be kept in step.

Presentation decisions duplicate across transform modules: shared furniture such as headers, navigation and footers is repeated in each transformer unless a logical page is introduced - the problem Two Step View solves.

The XSLT route brings toolchain costs: XSLT 1.0 limitations and processor dialect differences (Xalan, libxslt, XslCompiledTransform), stylesheets that must be compiled and cached, and debugging that happens through generated output rather than a debugger.
Per-response cost: building strings or DOM trees allocates and holds memory proportional to the page unless the transform streams.

participants.responsibility: Encapsulates the transformation for one domain type (or, in the XSLT realization, is the stylesheet): reads the domain data element by element and emits the markup for it. Stateless; a fresh instance or call per response.
The domain objects or record sets produced by the domain and data-source layers; the transformer reads their structure but is not coupled to how they were loaded.
The destination the markup is written to (response stream, PrintWriter, StringBuilder, XMLStreamWriter, SAX ContentHandler, fmt::Write); the transformer writes to it but does not own its lifecycle.
The page/front controller or responder that invokes the transformer with the model and commits the produced markup to the response; it owns request concerns such as content type, status and headers.
Declarative form of the transformer: a stylesheet applied by an XSLT processor to the serialized model, optionally parameterized per request.

use_cases: Generating XML or HTML fragments for machine consumers - feeds, sitemaps, export views - where no design workflow is involved and the markup shape is dictated by the data.
Rendering domain objects into markup in a service that also exposes the same data as JSON, so both representations are transformations of one model rather than two hand-maintained code paths.
Large or deeply structured documents (tables, trees, nested lists) whose markup structure follows the data, where template markers would need awkward loops and conditionals.
Server-side rendering in code-centric stacks (Node/TypeScript functions returning markup, Python ElementTree, Rust emitters) where the team prefers unit-testable functions over template files.
Multi-channel publishing where one domain model is transformed into several outputs (web HTML, XML for a partner, plain text for e-mail) through one transformer per channel.
Legacy XML pipelines where the domain is already serialized and an XSLT stylesheet per channel produces the presentation without touching application code.

XML publishing pipelines where each request flows through a generator, an XSLT transformer and a serializer: Apache Cocoon sitemaps wire those components per output format, so the presentation for each channel is a stylesheet applied to the serialized domain data.

Documentation toolchains where the authoring format is XML and the presentation is a stylesheet: the DocBook XSL stylesheets and the XSLT 3.0 DocBook xslTNG transform one DocBook document into HTML5, EPUB and print formats through per-element template rules.

Server-side HTML built from domain data by typed builder code instead of template files: Ktor's HTML DSL (kotlinx.html) generates responses by walking the model with type-safe Kotlin functions, a script-language Transform View unit-testable without an HTTP round-trip.
avoid_when: The markup is mostly static with a few holes for data: Template View is simpler and keeps the page editable by designers.
Designers or content editors must own the layout: use Template View or Two-Step View, where the page exists as an editable artifact.
One consistent site-wide look must be maintained and changed globally: Two-Step View factors the common layout out of the individual views.
A framework already generates markup from typed components (JSX/React, Razor, JSF, Vaadin, SwiftUI): use its component model instead of building a parallel transformation layer.
The output is a trivial interpolation of one or two fields: plain string formatting is enough and the transformer machinery is overhead.
anti_patterns: String-concatenating markup with unescaped user data, producing broken output and XSS.
One omnibus transformer that branches on page type (if page == artist ... else if page == album ...) instead of one transformer per domain type.
Choosing the mechanism by fashion: writing XSLT for logic that plain code expresses clearly, or hand-rolling markup when an XSLT stylesheet or a markup tree API already fits.
Transformers that read request, session or database state: a view that fetches data is no longer a pure transformation and cannot be tested or reused.
Duplicating the whole page furniture in every transformer with no shared logical page, so every global layout change touches every file.
Materializing the entire document in memory per response when the transform could stream.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: presentation transformation is distinct from request handling and from the domain logic that produces the data.
Single responsibility: one transformer per domain type and output format, invoked by composition rather than by branching.
Pure function / statelessness: transform(model) -> markup with no side effects on the model, which is what makes the view testable.
Open/closed principle: new output formats and channels arrive as new transformers, not as edits to existing ones or to their callers.
Don't repeat yourself: shared markup fragments and page furniture are factored out, not copy-pasted into every transformer.
Encapsulation of output encoding: escaping belongs in one writer or helper, not in every string concatenation.
best_practices: Write one transformer per domain type and output format; dispatch by type at the call site instead of branching inside a monolithic transformer.
Centralize escaping behind a helper or a writer API that escapes by default; never interpolate raw user data into markup.
Keep transformers pure - take the data, return or write the markup, no I/O or session access - so they stay unit-testable.
Stream large output to the response writer as you walk the domain instead of building the whole document in memory.
Test transformers with representative domain fixtures and compare normalized output, so escaping and structure regressions are caught.
If using XSLT: cache compiled stylesheets, pass per-request values as explicit parameters, and treat stylesheets as trusted code (untrusted stylesheets can read files and the network).
Factor shared page furniture into a logical page or shared fragments rather than duplicating it in every transformer.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Transform View, Web Presentation Patterns (chapter 14).
